steps.title: Asti and Alba
steps.body: Barbera's two main zones are Asti and Alba. Barbera d'Asti, a DOCG since 2008, is the larger zone, often lighter and fresher, with Nizza, a DOCG since 2014, as its top area. Barbera d'Alba, a DOC, grows on sites not given to Nebbiolo, giving fuller, richer wines.
steps.highlight: Barbera d'Asti and Nizza; Barbera d'Alba

steps.title: Beyond Piedmont
steps.body: Barbera grows in Lombardy's Oltrepò Pavese and Emilia-Romagna, where it's sometimes made fizzy. Italian immigrants took it to California and Argentina. Australia has small plantings. Its high acidity makes it useful in hot climates, where it keeps freshness.

steps.prompt: Match each zone to its Barbera.
steps.explanation: Each zone gives Barbera a different weight.

steps.body: Nizza is Barbera's top tier: a minimum of 18 months' ageing, 6 in wood, and grapes from the hills around Nizza Monferrato.

steps.prompt: Why is Barbera useful in hot climates?
steps.explanation: Its natural acidity keeps wines fresh even in heat.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barbera d'Asti and Nizza are DOCGs; Barbera d'Alba is richer
It also grows in Lombardy, Emilia, California and Argentina
Its acidity is useful in warm regions
